domain_judgments.rationale: Approximately one-quarter of intervention participants and one-fifth of controls lacked post-treatment or follow-up questionnaire data, and although mixed models included available observations and baseline symptoms did not predict completion, bias from outcome-dependent missingness was not ruled out.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Of those participants in the intervention group, 61% completed all eight lessons (25/41) and 76% completed post-treatment and three-month follow-up online assessments (31/41). A comparable proportion of the UC group completed post-treatment questionnaires at the end of the study period (i.e., one week after the cessation of the active intervention phase, 79%).

domain_judgments.rationale: The validated self-report outcomes were measured consistently across groups, but participants knew their allocation and the main outcomes were subjective and therefore potentially influenced by expectations; only telephone diagnostic interviewers were blinded.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: once randomization occurred, participants and study staff could not remain blinded to group allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered, the registry protocol was reportedly followed, and the prespecified primary and secondary outcomes were reported across the planned time points, providing little indication of selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The trial was prospectively registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN1261600024 9459), and the protocol was followed as per the registry.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is some concerns. The main issues are unclear allocation concealment and baseline imbalances, unblinded participants assessing subjective outcomes, possible intervention deviations, and roughly 21–24% missing questionnaire outcomes; prospective registration and broad outcome reporting reduce concern about selective reporting.
